units.title: Hello, Perl!
units.summary: Write your first Perl programs with print and say, and start every program with use strict and use warnings.

lesson.md: A program is a list of instructions for the computer. Perl runs them from top to bottom. You save a Perl program in a text file, for example `hello.pl`, and run it with the command `perl hello.pl`.

Your first instruction is `print`: it writes text on the screen. Text between double quotes is called a **string**. Inside a string, `\n` means a line break. Every statement ends with a semicolon `;`.

The first two lines are not output. `use strict;` makes Perl stop at common mistakes, for example a misspelled variable name. `use warnings;` makes Perl print a warning when your code looks suspicious. Start every program with these two lines.
`print` does not add a line break by itself. Without `\n`, the next `print` continues on the same line.

`say` works like `print`, but it adds a line break at the end. You turn it on once with the line `use feature 'say';` at the top of the program. The rest of this course uses `say` in almost every program.
`print` and `say` can show several values at once: separate them with commas. Numbers need no quotes, and Perl can calculate with `+`, `-`, `*` (multiply) and `/` (divide).
Perl is case-sensitive: `say` works, `Say` does not. A `#` starts a comment: Perl ignores everything from `#` to the end of the line.
A missing semicolon is the most common beginner mistake. Perl then reads two lines as one statement and stops with a `syntax error`.

card: `use strict;` and `use warnings;` start every program
`print "Hi\n";` prints text, `\n` is a line break
`say "Hi";` prints text and a line break

units.title: Scalars
units.summary: Store numbers and strings in scalar variables, put them into strings and calculate with them.

lesson.md: A variable is a name for a value. In Perl, a variable that holds one value is called a **scalar**. Its name starts with `$`, for example `$name`. The value can be a number or a string. `my` creates a new variable, and `=` stores a value in it.
Inside double quotes, Perl replaces a variable with its value. This is called **interpolation**. Single quotes keep the text exactly as written: no variables and no `\n`.

lesson.output:
I live in Paris.
I live in $city.

lesson.md: Perl calculates with `+`, `-`, `*` and `/`. `/` can give a decimal number. `%` gives the rest of a division, and `**` raises to a power. `$x += 3` is short for `$x = $x + 3`, and `$x++` adds 1.
The dot `.` joins two strings into one. The operator `x` repeats a string. `length` counts the characters of a string.
Perl changes between numbers and strings for you. The operator decides: `+` treats both values as numbers, `.` treats both values as strings. So `"3" + 4` is `7`, and `3 . 4` is `34`.
When letters follow a variable directly inside a string, put the name in braces: `"${fruit}s"` gives `apples` when `$fruit` is `"apple"`.
With `use strict`, you must create every variable with `my` before you use it. Otherwise Perl stops with the error `Global symbol "$total" requires explicit package name`.

exercises.explain: 17 divided by 5 is 3, with a rest of 2. `%` gives the rest.

Single quotes do not interpolate, so Perl prints the text exactly as written, including `$item`.
The dot `.` joins strings. Perl treats both values as strings, so the result is `53`.

units.title: Decisions
units.summary: Run code only when a condition is true with if, elsif, else and unless, and compare numbers and strings.

lesson.md: `if` runs a block of code only when a condition is true. The condition goes in parentheses, and the block goes in braces `{ }`. Both are required. `elsif` checks another condition when the first one is false (note the spelling), and `else` runs when no condition was true. You compare numbers with `==` (equal), `!=` (not equal), `<`, `>`, `<=` and `>=`.

Perl has separate operators to compare strings: `eq` (equal), `ne` (not equal), `lt` (comes first in alphabetical order) and `gt` (comes later). Use `==` for numbers and `eq` for strings. The number `10` and the number `10.0` are equal, but the strings `"10"` and `"10.0"` are different.

If you compare strings with `==`, Perl turns them into numbers first. A word without digits becomes `0`, so `"abc" == "xyz"` is true. `use warnings` then prints a warning. Always use `eq` for strings.

Perl has no special values for true and false. The number `0`, the empty string `""`, the string `"0"` and an undefined value are false. Every other value is true. `unless` is the opposite of `if`: it runs the block when the condition is false.
You combine conditions with `&&` (and: both must be true) and `||` (or: at least one must be true). `!` (not) turns true into false and false into true.
For a single statement, you can put `if` or `unless` after it. This short form needs no parentheses and no braces.

exercises.explain: 15 is not greater than 20, but it is greater than 10, so the `elsif` block runs.
The string `"0"` is false in Perl, so the `else` block runs.

units.title: Loops
units.summary: Repeat code with foreach, for and while, count with ranges like 1..5 and control loops with next and last.

lesson.md: A loop repeats a block of code. `foreach` runs the block once for every value in a list. `1..4` is a **range**: the numbers from 1 to 4. The variable after `my` holds the current value in each round.
`for` and `foreach` mean the same in Perl, and most people write the shorter `for`. A list can also be values in parentheses, separated by commas.

lesson.output:
I like apple
I like pear
I like plum

lesson.md: `while` repeats the block as long as the condition is true. Change something inside the loop, otherwise it never ends. `$n *= 3` is short for `$n = $n * 3`.
`for` also has a classic form with three parts, separated by semicolons: a start, a condition and a step that runs after each round. `$i -= 4` is short for `$i = $i - 4`.
`next` jumps to the next round at once. `last` ends the loop at once. Both are often used with the short `if` form.
A range always counts up, so `5..1` is an empty list. To count down, write `reverse 1..5`.

card: `while ($n < 10) { }` repeats while the condition is true
`next` jumps to the next round, `last` ends the loop

units.title: Arrays
units.summary: Keep many values in order in an array, add and remove items with push and pop, and use join and sort.

lesson.md: An **array** stores a list of scalars in a fixed order. Its name starts with `@`. You create it with a list in parentheses. Inside double quotes, an array prints its items with a space between them.

lesson.output:
apple banana cherry plum
apple
cherry
plum

lesson.md: Each item has an **index**, a position number that starts at `0`. One item is a scalar, so you write `$fruits[0]` with `$`, not `@`. A negative index counts from the end: `$fruits[-1]` is the last item.
`push` adds items at the end of an array. `pop` removes the last item and returns it, so you can store it in a variable.
You change an item with `=`. `scalar(@colors)` gives the number of items, and `$#colors` gives the last index.
`foreach` goes through the items of an array, one after the other.
`join` glues all items into one string, with a separator between them. `sort` returns a sorted copy of a list. By default, it sorts alphabetically.

`sort` compares strings by default, so `10` comes before `9`. To sort numbers, write `sort { $a <=> $b } @nums`. `$a` and `$b` are special variables that `sort` fills with two items, and `<=>` compares them as numbers.

units.title: Hashes
units.summary: Store pairs of keys and values in a hash, check keys with exists and loop over a hash in a fixed order.

lesson.md: A **hash** stores pairs of keys and values. You look up a value by its key, like a word in a dictionary. A hash name starts with `%`. Between a key and its value you write `=>`.
One value is a scalar, so you read it with `$` and the key in braces: `$ages{"Ann"}`. When the key is a simple word, you can leave out the quotes.
You add a new pair or change a value with `=`.
`exists` checks whether a key is in the hash. `delete` removes a key and its value.

lesson.output:

No entry for Peru

lesson.md: `keys %price` gives a list of all keys, and `values %price` a list of all values. A hash has no fixed order, and the order can change every time the program runs. For a fixed order, sort the keys: `sort keys %price`.

lesson.output:
cake costs 5
juice costs 4
tea costs 3

lesson.md: `scalar(keys %points)` counts the pairs. When the order does not matter, for example for a sum, you can use `values` directly.
A hash is great for counting. `my %count;` creates an empty hash. `$count{$w}++` adds 1 to the value of the key `$w`. A new key starts at 0.

card: `$h{Ann}` reads a value, `$h{Cy} = 40;` adds a pair

units.title: Subroutines
units.summary: Put code into reusable subroutines, pass arguments with @_ and give back results with return.

lesson.md: A **subroutine**, or sub, is a named block of code that you can run many times. You define it with `sub`, a name and a block in braces. You run, or **call**, it with its name and parentheses.

The values in the parentheses of a call are the **arguments**. Inside the sub, they are in the special array `@_`. `my ($name) = @_;` copies the first argument into a new variable. A variable created with `my` inside a sub exists only inside that sub.
`return` gives a value back to the caller. You can store the result in a variable or use it directly.
Do not forget the parentheses in `my ($name) = @_;`. Without them, `my $count = @_;` stores the number of arguments, because an array used as a single value gives its size.
`return` also ends the sub at once. This works well with the short `if` form.
A sub can take any number of arguments. When you pass an array, all its items go into `@_`.
A sub can also return a list. You catch the values with a list of variables in parentheses.

card: `sub name { ... }` defines a sub, `name();` calls it
`my` variables in a sub exist only inside it

15 is greater than 10, so the first call returns `big`. For 5, the first `return` is skipped and the sub returns `small`.
`$level` is created with `my` inside the sub, so it does not exist outside it. With `use strict`, Perl stops with an error.

units.title: Regular expressions
units.summary: Search text with patterns using =~ and m//, capture parts of a match and replace text with s///.

lesson.md: A **regular expression**, or regex, is a pattern that describes text. `=~` applies a pattern to a string. `m/Perl/`, or short `/Perl/`, is true when the text contains `Perl` anywhere. `!~` is true when the text does not match.
In a pattern, `^` means the start of the string and `$` means the end. The letter `i` after the pattern ignores the difference between upper and lower case.

Some characters have a special meaning. `\d` matches one digit, `\w` one letter, digit or `_`, and `\s` one space. A dot `.` matches any character, so write `\.` for a real dot. `+` after a character means one or more times, and `*` means zero or more times.

lesson.output:
2024 is a number
7 is a number

lesson.md: Parentheses in a pattern **capture** the part of the text they match. After a successful match, the first group is in `$1`, the second in `$2`, and so on. You can also assign the captured groups to a list of variables.
`s/old/new/` replaces the first match in a variable. The variable itself changes. With `g` at the end, it replaces every match.

lesson.output:
I like dogs. cats are nice.
I like dogs. dogs are nice.

lesson.md: The new text can use the captured groups. `s///` also returns the number of replacements.

card: `^` start, `$` end, `\d` digit, `\w` word character, `+` one or more

exercises.explain: `\d+` finds the first group of digits, `42`, and the parentheses capture it into `$1`.
`\.` matches a real dot, and `g` replaces every dot with `-`.
The pattern allows only digits from the start `^` to the end `$`. The other strings contain a space, letters or `!`.
Without `g`, `s///` replaces only the first match.
Patterns are case-sensitive: `world` does not match `World`. With `/world/i`, it would match.
